name: Horror
definition: Stories built to frighten: a threat that violates normal reality.
semantics: darkness, isolated locations, the unseen threat, vulnerable protagonists, mirrors/doors/corridors
syntax: knowledge gap between viewer and victim; threat withheld then revealed; safety repeatedly promised and broken

visual_signature.shot: wide shots with empty negative space behind the subject; reaction CU before the reveal
visual_signature.angle: eye-level for identification, Dutch for wrongness
visual_signature.movement: slow creeping push-ins, long static holds
visual_signature.lens: wide close-ups for distortion; deep focus so the background can hide something
visual_signature.pace: long holds then sudden cut (jump scare) - irregular rhythm

how: Show the space first so viewers search it; delay the threat; cut to the reaction before the reveal.

examples.note: fearful context is the strongest context effect on face reading - horror relies on context cuts

ai_image_prompt: dim corridor, single flickering ceiling light, wide shot with empty dark doorway behind a woman, low-key hard light, desaturated green-cyan grade, cinematic still
ai_video_prompt: slow creeping push-in down a dark corridor toward a half-open door, static long take, faint flicker, no sudden moves
check: Is the threat withheld for most of the runtime? Does the frame leave space for something to appear?

name: Thriller / suspense
definition: Tension from a likely bad outcome the audience can see coming.
syntax: audience knows more than the character (Hitchcock-style suspense); desirable outcome unlikely, undesirable likely (Carroll via Allen)

visual_signature.shot: inserts of the threat (timer, weapon); CU reactions
visual_signature.angle: eye-level; high angle on the trapped
visual_signature.lens: long lens compression for surveillance feel
visual_signature.colour: cool with one warm danger accent

how: Show the danger to the audience first (insert), then cut back to the unaware character; cross-cut rescuer and victim.
avoid_when: the stakes have not been set

examples.note: cross-cut rescue - suspense from likely bad vs unlikely good outcome
>65% of cortex correlated across viewers - very tight control of attention

ai_image_prompt: insert shot of a red digital timer under a cafe table, shallow depth of field, cool interior light, warm red glow, cinematic
ai_video_prompt: static insert of a timer counting down, then cut: a woman laughing at the table above, unaware
common_mistakes: surprise instead of suspense (hiding the danger from the audience)
check: Does the audience know the danger before the character?

name: Action
definition: Spectacle of physical conflict, chases, stunts.
syntax: goal + obstacle in physical form; escalation of set-pieces

visual_signature.shot: wide for geography, then MS/CU for impact
visual_signature.lens: wide close to action; telephoto for speed compression
visual_signature.colour: teal-orange is a common commercial look [CRAFT]
visual_signature.pace: short shots with high motion (ASL shortest of popular genres per Cutting-type corpora - genre detail not read)

how: Establish geography with one wide shot, keep screen direction of pursuer/pursued consistent, cut on action.

examples.note: shorter shots carry proportionately more motion in recent films

ai_image_prompt: low angle wide shot, motorbike skidding on wet neon street, motion blur, high contrast, cinematic action still
ai_video_prompt: tracking shot alongside a running courier left-to-right, handheld energy, fast
check: Can a viewer draw the chase map after one viewing?

name: Comedy (situational / physical)
definition: Built to amuse: incongruity, timing, character flaws.
syntax: setup -> expectation -> violation; reaction shot as the laugh trigger

visual_signature.shot: wide/full shots to see the body; reaction CU

how: Shoot gags wide and static; cut to the deadpan reaction; use smash cut for contradiction jokes.
avoid_when: sensitive topics (health anxiety) unless done kindly

examples.note: lower inter-subject correlation (18%) than tightly directed films; authors note it is often shot without a script
match-action substitution produces a striking comic effect

ai_image_prompt: full shot, a man frozen mid-slip on a shiny shop floor, bright high-key light, saturated colours, frontal flat staging
ai_video_prompt: static wide shot: a man slips and catches himself awkwardly, holds still, looks at the camera
check: Is the gag readable in one static shot?

name: Romantic comedy / romance
definition: Two people move toward each other through obstacles.
syntax: distance -> proximity; misunderstandings; final union

visual_signature.shot: two-shots; shot/reverse shot that tightens over the film
visual_signature.movement: gentle; slow push on the kiss/realisation
visual_signature.pace: modern remakes cut faster: You've Got Mail ~4 s ASL vs ~21 s in the 1940 original for the cafe scene

how: Start the couple far apart in frame and in separate singles; end in a shared two-shot.

examples.work: The Shop Around the Corner (1940) vs You've Got Mail (1998)
examples.note: same scene: 14 shots (~21 s) vs 84 shots (~4.3 s); the remake keeps continuity principles but narrows the range of framings

ai_image_prompt: two-shot in a small cafe, warm backlight through window, 85mm shallow depth of field, soft pastel palette
ai_video_prompt: slow push-in on two people at a cafe table as they both reach for the same cup
common_mistakes: singles throughout (no shared frame at the payoff)
check: Does the distance between the two shrink across the piece?

name: Drama / melodrama
definition: Character conflict and emotional change in realistic settings; melodrama heightens emotion and moral polarity.
syntax: desire vs obligation; revelation; sacrifice

visual_signature.shot: MCU/CU for performance; wides for isolation
visual_signature.light: naturalistic motivated; melodrama more stylised colour

how: Let reactions play; close-ups only on expressive beats; save the tightest shot for the turning point.

examples.note: sad close-up increased viewers' mental-state talk about the character

ai_image_prompt: medium close-up of an elderly man reading a letter at a kitchen table, soft window light, naturalistic colour
ai_video_prompt: static medium close-up, the man lowers the letter and looks out of the window, a slow breath
check: Where is the tightest shot? It should be the turning point.

name: Film noir / neo-noir
definition: Crime stories of moral ambiguity with a distinct high-contrast visual style.
semantics: night city, rain, venetian blinds, detectives, femme fatale, voice-over
syntax: flawed investigator, fatalism, entrapment

visual_signature.shot: MS/MCU with strong shadows; low-angle interiors
visual_signature.light: low-key (high contrast), spotted rather than flooded light, low/high direction shadows (Place & Peterson's terms)
visual_signature.colour: black and white or neon with deep blacks

how: One hard key, little fill (high ratio), shadows as shapes (blinds), practicals in frame.

examples.work: Film noir (as analysed by Place & Peterson 1976)
examples.note: described through Hollywood lighting terms: low key, spotted light, direction, highlight/shadow

ai_image_prompt: film noir still, detective in a dark office, hard single key light through venetian blinds casting striped shadows, low-key high contrast black and white
ai_video_prompt: static medium shot, smoke drifting through striped light from blinds, the man turns his head into the light
common_mistakes: filter on top of flat light (needs real contrast in the lighting)
check: Histogram: strong blacks and highlights, little midtone.

name: Western
definition: Frontier stories of law, land and individualism.
syntax: civilisation vs wilderness (Altman's example of a genre defined semantically and syntactically)

visual_signature.shot: extreme wides of landscape; extreme close-ups of eyes in standoffs
visual_signature.lens: wide for vistas; telephoto for heat-haze

how: Alternate EWS landscape with ECU eyes in a standoff; hold the tension then cut fast.

examples.work: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (Leone, 1966)
examples.note: evoked similar brain responses across viewers in ~45% of cortex; gaze clustered on the protagonist's actions

ai_image_prompt: extreme close-up of narrowed eyes under a hat brim, hard sun, warm dusty palette
ai_video_prompt: slow pan across a desert town at noon, heat haze, then hold on a lone figure
check: Scale contrast between EWS and ECU is present.

name: Science fiction
definition: Speculative technology/futures used to ask 'what if'.
syntax: human vs technology/system; discovery

visual_signature.shot: wides for world-building; ECU on interfaces
visual_signature.colour: cool blues/teals, clean whites or neon

how: Establish the world with one strong wide; let light come from in-world tech.

examples.note: Smith's examples of match-action, shot/reverse shot with clear screen locations, and gaze cues (owl sequence)

ai_image_prompt: wide shot of a rainy neon city street at night, holographic signs, cool teal palette with magenta accents, cinematic
ai_video_prompt: slow smooth push through a lab with glowing screens, cool light
common_mistakes: generic neon with no story logic
check: Does every light source exist in the world?

name: Fantasy / family animation
definition: Magical worlds and transformation, often aimed at families.
syntax: ordinary hero enters special world and returns changed

visual_signature.shot: varied; clear silhouettes

how: Clear silhouettes and staging; colour script that shifts with emotional arc.
ai_image_prompt: chibi boy with glasses discovers a glowing door in a forest, rim light, saturated colour, wide shot
ai_video_prompt: crane up revealing a glowing forest as the boy steps forward
check: Silhouette readable in black fill.

name: Observational documentary / vérité
definition: Filming real events with minimal intervention.
semantics: real people, real places, available light
syntax: discovery through watching; no staged conflict

visual_signature.shot: MS/WS handheld

how: Follow action, cut for clarity not style; let moments run.
avoid_when: when actions are staged and acting is weak (looks fake)

examples.work: Unedited one-shot video of Washington Square Park
examples.note: without directorial intervention, viewers' brain activity and gaze diverged (<5% cortex ISC) - observational footage needs framing/editing to guide attention

ai_image_prompt: handheld documentary still, optician adjusting frames for a customer, available window light, natural colour
ai_video_prompt: handheld follow shot of a staff member opening the shop in the morning
common_mistakes: no focal subject in a static wide (attention scatters)
check: Each shot has one clear subject.

name: Explainer / educational
definition: Video whose goal is understanding.
semantics: diagrams, talking head, screen recordings, text
syntax: question -> steps -> answer

visual_signature.shot: talking head MCU; diagram inserts
visual_signature.pace: segment by idea; cut pauses (jump cuts acceptable)

how: One idea per shot; signal changes with a consistent transition.
ai_image_prompt: clean diagram of the eye with lens, flat illustration, high contrast
check: One transition family; one idea per shot.

name: Music video / beat promo
definition: Image cut to music; mood and rhythm over plot.
syntax: visual rhythm mirrors musical structure

visual_signature.shot: varied sizes, punch-ins
visual_signature.pace: cut on beats; build to chorus

how: Map cuts to beats; save the biggest visual change for the drop/chorus.
check: Cut density changes between verse and chorus.

name: Classical continuity style
definition: Invisible editing: establishing shot, coverage, shot/reverse shot, 180-degree system, eyeline and action matches.
syntax: space and time made clear so the story dominates

visual_signature.shot: establishing -> MS -> CU as the scene intensifies

how: Master scene + coverage; cut on looks, lines and action; keep screen positions.
use_when: anything where the viewer must follow who/where

examples.note: Bordwell's classical model: longer takes, more variety of camera distance

check: Line not crossed unintentionally; eyelines meet.

name: Intensified continuity
definition: Contemporary mainstream style: rapid cutting, tight singles in dialogue, more reaction/POV shots, free-moving camera - still obeying continuity logic.
syntax: continuity rules kept; pace and closeness increased

visual_signature.shot: OTS and tight singles
visual_signature.movement: free-ranging camera, long virtuoso travelling shots as exceptions
visual_signature.pace: ASL ~2-4 s in post-1960s US films per Bordwell; ~4 s in You've Got Mail sections

how: Cover every line and reaction; cut fast; keep screen positions very consistent so the speed doesn't confuse.
purpose: Engagement, momentum; dominant mass-audience style and the base of short-form vertical editing.
avoid_when: scenes needing performance continuity or contemplation

examples.note: 84 shots (~4.3 s) for a scene the 1940 original did in 14
praised by Bordwell as intelligent use of the style
intensified continuity produced strong attentional synchrony regardless of comprehension

common_mistakes: fast cutting with inconsistent screen positions
check: Every cut has an attention cue.

name: Long-take staging in depth
definition: Scenes played in few, long shots; attention guided by blocking (actor movement, position in depth, light) instead of cuts.
syntax: the frame is a stage; the viewer chooses within limits

visual_signature.shot: WS/MS with depth
visual_signature.light: pools of light leading the eye

how: Block actors so the important one moves, faces camera, or is in the light when it matters; use entrances and turns as 'cuts'.
purpose: Realism, performance, tension of the uninterrupted.
avoid_when: AI video beyond the model's clip length

examples.work: Long-take/deep-focus traditions (Welles is named by Smith 2012)
examples.note: cited as the alternative to analytical editing

ai_video_prompt: single continuous shot, the camera slowly tracks as the customer walks from the door to the counter, staff turns to greet her
common_mistakes: no motion cue so viewers look at the wrong person
check: Gaze test: where would 10 viewers look at each second? (motion, faces, light)

name: Observational / handheld immediacy
definition: Camera reacts to events like an observer; framing imperfect on purpose.
syntax: discovery

visual_signature.shot: MS

how: Camera searches and finds; allow reframing; avoid perfect symmetry.
ai_video_prompt: 'handheld camera, slight natural shake, follows the person, imperfect framing'
common_mistakes: shake so strong it causes discomfort (see whip-pan OKR note)
check: Subject stays readable.

name: Formalist / symmetrical tableau
definition: Flat, centred, symmetrical frames, planimetric staging, controlled colour; camera moves on straight axes.
syntax: the world as a composed diorama; emotion under control

visual_signature.shot: frontal MS/WS

how: Centre the subject, align background parallel to the sensor, limit palette to 3-4 colours. Describe by technique; do not name or imitate a specific living director.
ai_image_prompt: perfectly symmetrical frontal shot of a small optician shop counter, centred figure, pastel palette, flat even light, planimetric composition
ai_video_prompt: static symmetrical frame, then a straight lateral track to the next room
check: Vertical centre line and horizon exact.

name: Expressive montage (Soviet tradition)
definition: Meaning created by the collision/juxtaposition of shots rather than continuity of space.
syntax: shot A + shot B = idea C (Kuleshov-type juxtaposition)

visual_signature.shot: strong graphic shots

how: Pair shots for an idea; use graphic contrast (direction, scale, tone) between consecutive shots.

examples.note: juxtaposition shifts the reading of a face, but effects are moderate and not universal (null in Prince & Hensley 1992)

common_mistakes: assuming juxtaposition alone carries the meaning
check: Would 3 viewers state the same idea?

name: Slow / contemplative cinema
definition: Very long takes, little dialogue, attention to time and environment.
syntax: duration as meaning

visual_signature.shot: WS/EWS static

how: Hold beyond comfort; let small changes (light, wind) be events.
avoid_when: feed openings (first seconds need a reason to stay)
ai_video_prompt: static wide shot, clouds drifting over a mountain lake, nothing else moves
check: At least one small change every few seconds.
